title: The fakes

story: A cloud change adds a small status badge to each site on the projects page: ready, unhealthy or offline. To get it, the cloud asks the site's on-prem client, the Rhino software that runs inside the customer's network, for a health check. The pull request has a test, and the test replaces the cloud's client for those calls with a mock that answers {"is_healthy": True}. The test is green, a person approves, and the change ships.

In production the badge breaks for every site with TypeError: 'HealthCheckResponse' object is not subscriptable. The real client never returns a dictionary; it returns a protobuf message, and the code read it like a dictionary because that is what the mock taught it. fcp's cloud tests replace that client with a mock in 69 places, and every one of them answers what its author believed the client returns.
hook.question: How can a test talk to an on-prem client that is not there, and still run the cloud's real client code and the real bytes on the wire?

read.h: A mock replaces the very code you need to test
p: Here is the test from the story, reduced to its core. patch swaps the class AgentClient for a MagicMock, the Python cousin of vi.fn(), and the mock's call method returns a dictionary. So the test runs site_status with everything below it removed: the real client, the encoding of the request into bytes, the answer coming back and the decoding into a HealthCheckResponse. The one assumption that was wrong, the shape of the answer, is the one thing the test made up. That is the general weakness of mocks at a boundary: they check that your code agrees with your own idea of the other side.

The fakes lesson showed the alternative for an object store: a fake, a small real implementation that keeps its state in memory and behaves like the real service. This lesson applies it to the hardest of the cloud's three outside parts, the on-prem client, which the cloud reaches over gRPC, a way to call functions on another machine where a .proto file describes every message. The goal is a fake that sits behind the wire, so the cloud's real client, the real protobuf encoding and a real socket are all part of every test.

read.h: Put the fake on the far side of the wire
p: Start from how the cloud really talks to a client. Every call goes through one gRPC method on a proxy service, AgentRpc, and its request carries three things: which client (the agent ID), which method (a name such as HealthCheck), and that method's own request, already turned into bytes. The answer comes back the same way, as bytes plus an error message and an error type. The proto file in the lab copies that shape on a small scale.

gRPC generates two pieces of Python code from a proto file: a stub, which the client uses to make calls, and a servicer, a base class that a server implements. The fake is a servicer. It runs as a real gRPC server inside the test process, it decodes the request bytes with the real message type, answers from memory, and encodes the reply. To decide how to decode, it looks the method name up in the proto's own description of the Agent service, which is the same lookup the cloud's client does to decode the answer. Nothing in the production code changes: a fixture starts the server on port 0, which means any free port, and points the real client at it through the setting the client reads, exactly where production code meets the network. That place is called the seam.

A servicer: the generated base class for the server side of the proxy.
Every call is recorded, so a test can check which client was asked for what.
An offline client: the answer the real proxy gives when a client is not connected, an error type, not an exception.
A method the fake does not know fails with its name. The next section says why.
Real decoding: the bytes the real client produced, read with the real message type.
Real encoding on the way back, so the real client decodes a real HealthCheckResponse.

read.h: Loud about gaps, true to the real errors
p: A fake is only useful if it is honest, and two habits keep it honest. The first is to be loud about gaps. fcp's client offers dozens of methods and the fake implements only the handful the first tests need. When code under test calls a method the fake does not know, the fake answers with an error that names the method, so the test fails with "does not implement GetEnvironmentVariable" and whoever reads it knows exactly what to add. A fake that quietly returned an empty answer would turn every missing method into a test that passes for the wrong reason.

The second habit is to fail the way the real thing fails. When a client is not connected, the real proxy does not throw; it answers with the error type TIMEOUT, and the cloud's client turns that into its own exception. So the fake keeps a set of offline agents and answers them with TIMEOUT too, and the cloud code's handling of offline sites is tested through the same path as in production.

code.text:
@pytest.fixture
def agents(monkeypatch):
    fake = FakeAgents()
    server = grpc.server(futures.ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=2))
    add_AgentProxyServicer_to_server(fake, server)
    port = server.add_insecure_port("127.0.0.1:0")  # 0: any free port
    server.start()
    monkeypatch.setenv("AGENT_PROXY_ADDRESS", f"127.0.0.1:{port}")  # the seam: where the real client looks
    yield fake
    server.stop(None)


def test_an_agent_that_is_not_connected_is_offline(agents):
    agents.offline.add("agent-2")
    assert sites.site_status("agent-2") == "offline"

notes.text: A real gRPC server in this process, with our fake as the proxy service.
Port 0: the operating system picks a free port, so parallel tests never collide.
The seam. The real client reads this address every time one is created.
The test describes the world (this agent is not connected), not what the code should call.

deeper.h: Go deeper: finishing a task on the test's thread
p: In fcp a task, such as importing a dataset, is scheduled on a client with a ScheduleTask call, and the client later reports the result, which the cloud handles in a separate job. The fake's handlers run on the gRPC server's thread, outside the test's database transaction, so they never touch the database; anything they wrote there would not be rolled back with the test.

So finishing a task is an explicit step in the test. The fake records each scheduled task, and the test calls complete_task(task_uid, status, output), which runs the cloud's real task-response handler, the same code the background job runs in production, on the test's own thread. The test decides when the client "finishes", and the cloud's own code updates the dataset's status. The next lesson uses this to build datasets through the API.

read.h: A contract suite keeps the fake honest
p: Real clients change, and fakes get "simplified" by people in a hurry, so a fake needs the same protection as in the fakes lesson: a contract suite, one set of tests that describes how the other side behaves and runs against the fake and against the real thing. For the on-prem client the contract is short: a health check answers, an unknown agent gets the timeout error type, a scheduled task shows up and its response is handled. The tests carry the marker contract, so pytest -m contract runs only them.

The real side is harder to reach than a MinIO container, because a real client needs the whole product around it. That is what FCP Lab is for, the full product on one machine with fake seed data. The contract suite takes an option, --target, which is fake by default and lab when it should point the client settings at a running Lab. Every pull request then checks the fake against a real client automatically, which a later lesson in this part sets up.

deeper.h: Go deeper: the other two fakes
p: The object store is the fakes lesson's lab in fcp's shape: an in-memory provider class that implements every method of the cloud's storage provider base class, put in place where the storage service creates its provider. One extra seam is needed, because the cloud downloads presigned links with requests.get, so the fixture also answers links to a made-up host from memory. Its contract suite runs on the fake and on MinIO, which the cloud's CI job already starts.

The task queue fake replaces Celery's send step instead of running tasks at once. Today some unit tests set CELERY_TASK_ALWAYS_EAGER, which runs a task inside the caller at the moment it is sent, so the code never sees work that is queued but not yet done. The fake records each task when the code sends it, after passing the arguments through the same serializer the broker uses, and runs nothing until the test calls drain(), oldest first, following chains of tasks. Its contract suite runs the same scenarios on a real Celery worker with Redis.

lab.title: A fake on-prem agent behind a real gRPC socket
needs: No Docker: the fake runs inside the test process
lab.goal: Watch a mock pass the bug from the story, then replace it with a fake gRPC server that the real client talks to, and make the fake loud about what it does not know.

guess.q: site_status reads health["is_healthy"]. The mock test makes the client return {"is_healthy": True}. A second test uses a fake gRPC server and the real client. What happens?

options.text: Both pass, because both answer is_healthy true.
options.why: The values agree, but the types do not. Only the fake goes through the real client, which returns a protobuf message.

options.text: The mock test passes and the fake test fails with TypeError, exactly like production.
options.why: The real client decodes the bytes into a HealthCheckResponse, and a protobuf message cannot be read with square brackets.

options.text: Both fail, because no real on-prem client is running.
options.why: Neither test needs a real client. The mock removes it; the fake stands in for it behind a real socket.

follow.say: Write the proto, a small copy of the cloud's proxy: one AgentRpc call that carries a method name and that method's request as bytes. Then generate the Python code.
Write the production code: the cloud's client, which reads the proxy address from the environment like fcp reads it from settings, and the status function from the story, bug included.
Write the mock test from the story and run it. It is green.
Now the fake, a real gRPC server that answers from memory, and a fixture that starts it on a free port and points the real client at it.
follow.do:
cat > fake_agents.py <<'EOF'
"""A fake on-prem agent behind the real proxy contract. The cloud's real AgentClient talks to it over a real socket."""
import agent_pb2 as pb
from agent_pb2_grpc import AgentProxyServicer

METHODS = pb.DESCRIPTOR.services_by_name["Agent"].methods_by_name  # method name -> its request type


class FakeAgents(AgentProxyServicer):
    def __init__(self):
        self.calls: list[tuple[str, str]] = []
        self.offline: set[str] = set()
        self.scheduled: list[pb.ScheduleTaskRequest] = []

    def AgentRpc(self, request, context):
        self.calls.append((request.agent_id, request.method_name))
        if request.agent_id in self.offline:
            return pb.AgentRpcResponse(error_type=pb.AgentRpcResponse.TIMEOUT, error_message="agent not connected")
        handler = getattr(self, f"_{request.method_name}", None)
        if handler is None:  # loud on purpose: a gap fails the test instead of passing quietly
            return pb.AgentRpcResponse(error_message=f"FakeAgents does not implement {request.method_name}")
        request_type = getattr(pb, METHODS[request.method_name].input_type.name)
        reply = handler(request_type.FromString(request.request_data))
        return pb.AgentRpcResponse(response_data=reply.SerializeToString())

    def _HealthCheck(self, request):
        return pb.HealthCheckResponse(is_healthy=True)
EOF

lab.build: Starting a dataset import schedules a task on the site's client. Add start_import(agent_id, dataset_uid) to sites.py: it builds a ScheduleTaskRequest with task_uid f"import-{dataset_uid}", task_type "DATASET_IMPORT" and the dataset_uid, sends it with AgentClient().call(agent_id, "ScheduleTask", request, pb.Empty) and returns the task_uid. Run a test for it first and read the loud error. Then teach the fake ScheduleTask: a _ScheduleTask handler that appends the decoded request to self.scheduled and returns pb.Empty(). Write tests/test_import.py, which starts an import of ds-7 and asserts that exactly one task was scheduled, with the right task_uid, task_type and dataset_uid, read from the fake. Finally break your own code on purpose: send pb.HealthCheckRequest() instead of the ScheduleTaskRequest and see the test fail, because the bytes no longer decode into the fields you expected.
checks: uv run pytest -q passes, and there is no mock left in tests/.
Before you added _ScheduleTask, the import test failed with "FakeAgents does not implement ScheduleTask".
test_import.py reads the task from agents.scheduled, which the fake filled from real bytes, not from your arguments.
Sending the wrong message type makes the import test fail with empty fields ('', '', '').
The offline test passes without any try or except in the test itself.

solution.file: sites.py, fake_agents.py and tests/test_import.py (the new parts)
solution.text:
# sites.py
def start_import(agent_id: str, dataset_uid: str) -> str:
    task_uid = f"import-{dataset_uid}"
    request = pb.ScheduleTaskRequest(task_uid=task_uid, task_type="DATASET_IMPORT", dataset_uid=dataset_uid)
    AgentClient().call(agent_id, "ScheduleTask", request, pb.Empty)
    return task_uid


# fake_agents.py, inside class FakeAgents
    def _ScheduleTask(self, request):
        self.scheduled.append(request)
        return pb.Empty()


# tests/test_import.py
import sites


def test_an_import_schedules_one_task_on_the_site(agents):
    task_uid = sites.start_import("agent-1", "ds-7")
    [task] = agents.scheduled
    assert (task.task_uid, task.task_type, task.dataset_uid) == (task_uid, "DATASET_IMPORT", "ds-7")

What is the seam in this lab, and why does the fake go there instead of replacing AgentClient?
Why does an offline agent get a TIMEOUT answer from the fake instead of a Python exception?

check.q: Why does the fake implement the proxy's servicer instead of replacing the cloud's AgentClient class with a stand-in?

options.text: So the real client code, the protobuf encoding and a real socket are part of every test.
options.why: Everything above the wire stays production code. A replaced client would hide exactly the bug from the story.

options.text: Because AgentClient cannot be patched in Python.
options.why: It can, and 69 tests do. That is the problem: patching it removes the code you want to test.

options.text: Because a gRPC server is faster than a mock.
options.why: A mock is faster. The fake wins on honesty, not speed.

check.q: The fake receives a call for GetTensorBoardLogsMetadata, which it does not implement yet. What should it do?

options.text: Return an empty answer, so the test can go on.
options.why: An empty answer decodes into a message full of defaults, and a test can pass for the wrong reason. The gap stays hidden.

options.text: Raise an exception inside the server thread.
options.why: The real proxy answers with an error, it does not crash. An exception on the server thread is also hard to read in the test output.

options.text: Answer with an error message that names the method, so the test fails and says exactly what to add.
options.why: A loud gap is a short to-do item: add the handler and a contract case for it.

check.q: What keeps the fake from slowly drifting away from the real on-prem client?

options.text: Code review of every change to the fake.
options.why: Reviews help, but nobody can see from a diff that the real client changed its behaviour last week.

options.text: A contract suite that runs the same tests against the fake and, with --target lab, against a real client in FCP Lab.
options.why: When the real side behaves differently, the same test fails on one target and passes on the other, and that difference is the drift.

options.text: Generating the fake from the proto file.
options.why: The proto gives the message shapes, not the behaviour, such as what an offline client answers.

p: FakeOnPremClient in cloud/rhinoCloud/tests_api/fakes/onprem_client.py subclasses RhinoCloudInternalRpcProxyServicer from common/fcp_common/rhinoAgentRpc and decodes request_data with the RhinoAgentRpc service descriptor, the same lookup AgentRpcClient uses. The onprem_client fixture starts grpc.server on 127.0.0.1:0 and monkeypatches AGENT_RPC_INTERNAL_CLOUD_PROXY_DNS and AGENT_RPC_INTERNAL_CLOUD_PROXY_PORT. The first handlers are HealthCheck, SystemStatus, ScheduleTask, GetEnvironmentVariable, GetAgentGcpProjectId, ValidateDatasetImportPaths and GetTensorBoardLogsMetadata; offline_agents answers TIMEOUT, and complete_task() runs handle_task_response, the code task_response_job runs. The mocks in rhinoCore/tests stay as they are.

InMemoryStorageProvider replaces AWSStorageServiceProvider where StorageService builds it and patches storage_service.requests.get for http://object-store.fake; its contract suite runs on MinIO in the API Tests job. FakeTaskQueue replaces app.send_task, serializes arguments with kombu (loads needs prepare_accept_content(app.conf.accept_content)), and drain() follows Celery chains; its contract suite uses start_worker with Redis. The contract suites carry the marker contract, and the on-prem one runs against FCP Lab with --target lab from the PR smoke job.

tickets.why: FakeOnPremClient behind the real gRPC proxy contract, its fixture, complete_task and its contract suite: this lesson.
The in-memory object store and its contract suite against MinIO (the fakes lesson in fcp's shape).
FakeTaskQueue: record, then drain, through the real serializer, with a contract suite on a real Celery worker.

words.plain: A small working stand-in for a real service that keeps state in memory and behaves like the real one.
The class gRPC generates for the server side of a service; a fake server implements it.
The one place where production code reaches the real service; the fake is put in there and nowhere else.
A fake's error that names a method it does not implement, so a missing piece fails a test instead of passing.
Tests that describe the other side's behaviour and run against both the fake and the real thing.

review.q: Explain in two sentences why 69 mocks of the client are a risk even when every test is green.
review.a: Each mock answers what its author believed the client returns, and it removes the real client, encoding and decoding from the test. When reality differs, the tests stay green and production breaks.

review.q: Name the two habits that keep a fake honest, with one example each.
review.a: Be loud about gaps (an unknown method answers with an error that names it) and fail like the real thing (an offline client answers TIMEOUT, as the real proxy does). Plus a contract suite run against the real side.

review.q: Why do the fake's handlers never write to the database, and how does a test finish a task?
review.a: They run on the gRPC server's thread, outside the test's transaction, so their writes would not be rolled back. The test calls complete_task, which runs the real task-response handler on the test's own thread.

remember: Put the fake behind the wire, so the real client and the real bytes run in every test, and make it fail loudly and the way the real thing fails.
